# Probability the Second Player Wins on $\omega_1$

## Setting Up the Problem

The "set of the first uncountable ordinal" is $\omega_1 = \{\alpha : \alpha \text{ is a countable ordinal}\}$, which has cardinality $\aleph_1$.

We need a natural probability measure on $\omega_1$. The key structural feature of $\omega_1$ is:

> **For every $\alpha \in \omega_1$, the initial segment $[\alpha) = \{\beta : \beta < \alpha\}$ is *countable*, while the tail $(\alpha, \omega_1) = \{\beta : \beta > \alpha\}$ has cardinality $\aleph_1$ (the "full" size of $\omega_1$).**

The natural probability measure is one in which **countable subsets have probability 0** and **uncountable subsets have probability 1**. This is the only measure consistent with the ordinal structure (there is no countable "base" to build a measure from, unlike $[0,1]$ or $\mathbb{N}$).

## Analyzing the Game

Let $X$ be the first player's hit and $Y$ the second player's hit. I need $P(Y > X)$.

**Condition on any outcome $X = \alpha$** (where $\alpha$ is some countable ordinal):

| Event | Set of outcomes for $Y$ | Cardinality | Probability |
|---|---|---|---|
| $Y < \alpha$ (first player wins) | $[\alpha)$ | **Countable** | $0$ |
| $Y = \alpha$ (tie) | $\{\alpha\}$ | **Countable** | $0$ |
| $Y > \alpha$ (second player wins) | $(\alpha, \omega_1)$ | $\aleph_1$ (uncountable) | $1$ |

The critical observation: **no matter which ordinal $\alpha$ the first player hits**, the set of ordinals that fail to beat $\alpha$ is countable (probability 0), while the set of ordinals that *do* beat $\alpha$ is co-countable (probability 1).

This is a complete asymmetry — fundamentally different from, say, throwing darts at $[0,1]$ where both the lower and upper intervals have positive probability.

## Conclusion

Since for **every** possible outcome $\alpha$ of the first player:

$$P(Y > X \mid X = \alpha) = P(Y \in (\alpha,\, \omega_1)) = 1,$$

we obtain:

$$P(Y > X) = 1.$$

The second player wins with certainty.

$$\boxed{1}$$
